blocks.text: The Earth was already diverse before states and civilizations emerged. Valleys, mountains, grasslands, islands and monsoon regions imposed different costs on obtaining water, food and transport. Different conditions, however, did not predetermine political institutions or historical outcomes.

Water supports life while creating organizational demands. Reliable supplies, seasonal rainfall and irrigation requiring maintenance present different problems of cooperation. A river can also serve as a transport route linking distant settlements. It cannot, by itself, accomplish political integration.

Agricultural systems connect land, labor, seasons and storage in different ways, supporting different population densities and patterns of surplus. Whether surplus can accumulate depends on distribution, maintenance and exchange. Neither a particular crop nor an environment entails a single social form.

People alter these conditions through technology, migration and institutions. Geography changes the questions societies face and the costs of answering them; it does not supply the answers. Civilizational divergence emerges through continuing interactions between environments and societies, and similar conditions can sustain different paths.
